**Playbook for ref_commons**

- When the game is a shared renewable stock with a fixed number of seasons, my default each season is the announced sustainable share per boat. It keeps the stock at cap and pays out every round. Matching it exactly worked for five straight seasons in practice.

- Watch the other boats' reported catches each season. If everyone is at the sustainable share and the stock holds steady, keep matching it exactly. Cooperation is stable and profitable; don't be the first to defect while many seasons remain.

- If one boat overfishes but the stock stays well above zero, I do not need to retaliate immediately. A single defection (boat 1 took 15.0 in season 5) cost me little and cooperation otherwise held. Retaliation only makes sense if it prevents future overfishing with enough seasons left to matter.

- In the FINAL season, conservation value is zero — take everything the stock can support. I took the whole remaining stock (94.2) in season 6 with no penalty and it capped my score at 117.5. Don't take a token amount above sustainable; take it all.

- Before submitting a final-season grab, check whether the stock is large enough that one boat can't take it all or whether catches are capped. If there's an explicit maximum or a per-boat limit, take that maximum. If others might race me to it, still grab the largest amount available — a share of a rushed collapse beats a polite share of nothing. In this episode no cap existed and no one else raced me; the full stock was mine.

- Defecting one season early (second-to-last round) is worth reconsidering more seriously: a defection DID occur in season 5 here, and I missed it. If any boat has already broken cooperation, or if I suspect the endgame grab is coming, defecting in the second-to-last round costs little (the stock barely dipped: 94.2 vs 100) and adds materially to my total. Default stays cooperative through the penultimate round, but treat any observed overfishing as the trigger to defect one round early alongside them.

- The endgame grab works best when the stock is near cap — which is exactly what cooperation buys me. Keep the stock healthy precisely so the final-season liquidation is worth more.

- The announced "sustainable share" line is a reliable guide mid-game: when the stock was at 100 it read 11.1, when it fell to 94.2 it read 10.5. I can trust that number as my cooperative benchmark without recomputing the growth model myself.

- General rule: keep me even with competitors in all middle rounds, harvest everything when the horizon ends. My total is what's scored, not the stock I leave behind.

**Playbook for shared-stock fishery games**

- On the first season, I submit the stated sustainable share (or just under it). This signals cooperation and tests whether others do the same.

- If the posted history shows all boats landing at or below the sustainable share and the stock holding steady, I keep matching the sustainable share every season. Cooperation held perfectly through season 4 in my run; do not defect early — an early overcatch risks triggering retaliation and collapse for many remaining seasons.

- I watch the history each season for two things: whether anyone has defected, and whether the stock is dropping. If another boat overcatches but the stock stays near max, I stay cooperative rather than retaliating — one defection doesn't justify abandoning a stable arrangement.

- In the second-to-last season, defect with a modest overcatch (roughly 30–40% above the sustainable share, e.g. 15 vs. 11.1). This worked in practice: I gained ~4 fish, the stock only fell to ~94, and no one retaliated. Others appeared to keep cooperating even after my defection, so the endgame grab is essentially free.

- In the final season, there is no future to protect, so I take more than the sustainable share — but only modestly more (a few units above the share, e.g. ~14 vs. a share of ~10.5). Note that my own prior defection lowered the final-season sustainable share slightly, but the two endgame defections together still netted clearly positive. Keep both.

- Never defect in an early or middle season when others are cooperating. In my run the cooperative equilibrium held at ~11/boat for the whole mid-game; the only extra points came from endgame defections, which cost almost nothing.

- If the stock ever drops sharply or someone defects early, I reassess: defect in kind to avoid being exploited, but keep catches moderate so the stock survives to the last season.

- General rule: compute total expected fish across remaining seasons, not per-season greed. Protecting the stock dominates until there are ≤2 seasons left.

- Check the endgame timing carefully: with N seasons, the defection window is seasons N-1 and N only. Confirm from the header how many seasons remain before submitting — the header always states it, so there is no excuse for misjudging the last rounds.

- Calibrate the size of the endgame defection to what the stock can absorb: after the season-5 grab of 15 the stock only fell ~6 points, so a slightly larger grab (15–18) would likely have been safe. Err toward the larger end of "modest" in the endgame, since no one retaliated within the remaining seasons.

2.text:
When the season prompt is put to me, I first check the current stock and the stated sustainable share, and I check the history of what the other boats actually landed.

While stock is at or near its cap and others are landing at the sustainable level, I submit exactly the sustainable share each season. This keeps the stock at max and preserves future seasons. This worked for five straight seasons: my restraint cost nothing because the stock stayed at 100.

If others overfish once, I do not panic-defect immediately; a single defection only dropped the stock from 100 to 94, which was still healthy. Match the quota again next season and watch whether it repeats.

If another boat overfishes in the second-to-last season, that is a signal it will fish hard in the last season too. In the final season I should not just take "a third" — take as large a catch as I plausibly can, since a greedy rival will take theirs regardless and leftover stock is pure waste to me.

On the final season, when no future remains, conservation has zero value: submit the largest catch I can, not the sustainable share and not a token bump. My final take of 35 (leaving only a small residue after the others) was the right scale — roughly a third of the remaining stock again works as a floor, but aim high; the harvest mechanism will cap me at what is actually there. Do not be timid on the last round.

Do not be a pure sucker: if another boat takes above quota repeatedly, I take my revenge in kind while the stock still supports it, rather than subsidizing their overfishing with my restraint. My score is only my own landed fish, so once cooperation cannot be enforced, per-season I maximize my own catch, not group totals.

Note the timing asymmetry: a defection by a rival late in the game is more dangerous to me than an early one, because I have fewer seasons to earn back the loss. From season 5 onward, if a rival overfishes, consider raising my own catch the very next season rather than waiting for the final round.

Sizing a big final catch: aim for something on the order of the whole remaining stock minus what I expect the rivals to take (assume a defector takes at least half again their quota). If I undershoot, the leftover is pure loss; if I overshoot, I am presumably capped at what exists. Bias high, not low.

Keep replies brief and always end with the required bracketed token.
